nameStory: The name 'pollock' comes from the Scottish word 'pollack,' which may derive from 'poll' meaning head, possibly referring to this fish's distinctive large head and eyes. In Britain, this same fish is called 'coalfish' because of its dark, coal-like coloration, especially when young.
description: Pollock are sleek, torpedo-shaped members of the cod family that can grow quite large, sometimes reaching over 3 feet long. They have a distinctive dark olive-green to brownish back that fades to silver on the sides and belly. Their most notable feature is a prominent lower jaw that juts out slightly beyond the upper jaw, giving them a somewhat aggressive appearance. Unlike their cod cousins, pollock have a more streamlined, athletic build perfect for chasing prey in open water.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: The lower jaw extends noticeably beyond the upper jaw, creating an underbite that feels firm and bony when touched. This protruding lower jaw is the pollock's signature feature.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark olive-green to brownish back with bright silver sides that feel smooth and slightly slimy. The contrast between the dark back and silver belly is sharp and unmistakable.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined and torpedo-shaped with a muscular feel, more athletic-looking than the chunky cod. The body tapers smoothly from head to tail with no obvious humps or curves.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Three separate dorsal fins on the back and two anal fins underneath, all feeling relatively soft to the touch. The tail fin has a slight fork and appears proportionally larger than a cod's.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Commonly caught at 1-2 feet long, but can grow much larger up to 3+ feet. Feels surprisingly heavy and solid for its size due to muscular build.

habitat: Pollock prefer the cooler waters off New England's rocky coasts and around underwater structures like reefs, wrecks, and ledges. They're typically found in deeper waters than cod, often 50-200 feet down, though they'll come closer to shore in spring and fall. Look for them around the Gulf of Maine, Cape Cod waters, and anywhere there's good current flow over rocky bottom.

seasonality.spring: Pollock move closer to shore for spawning, making them more accessible to anglers. This is when you'll see the largest concentrations near coastal waters.
seasonality.summer: Adults retreat to deeper, cooler waters offshore. Younger pollock may still be found around shallow rocky areas and kelp beds.
seasonality.fall: Another peak time as pollock follow baitfish schools back toward shore. Their feeding activity increases as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Most pollock move to deeper offshore waters where temperatures are more stable. Ice fishing is generally not productive for this species.

funFact: Pollock are such efficient swimmers that they can leap completely out of the water when hooked, earning them the nickname 'the acrobat of the cod family' - a behavior almost never seen in their chunky cod relatives.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with cod, but remember the jaw trick: pollock have an underbite (lower jaw sticks out), while cod have an overbite (upper jaw extends further). Pollock are also more streamlined and darker on top, while cod are chunkier with a more mottled, lighter appearance.
contextualKnowledge: In New England, this fish is always called 'pollock,' but the same species goes by 'coalfish' or 'saithe' in Britain. Don't confuse it with Alaskan pollock from the Pacific - that's actually a completely different species despite sharing the common name.
compareHints: Since pollock is the only species in its genus found in New England waters, compare it to its cod family relatives. Unlike the chunky Atlantic cod with its barbel (chin whisker) and mottled pattern, pollock are sleeker with no barbel and solid dark backs. Haddock have a distinctive black lateral line and thumb-print spot that pollock lack entirely.
